connector: Kirsti needs a new button, so the girls go to Mrs. Hirsch’s little shop on the corner. But something has changed. Today’s chapter is full of small objects that carry big news: a lock, a sign, a knock at night. Read each one like a warning.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Grete. Today a broken button sends the girls to a little shop they’ve known all their lives. What they find there changes how Annemarie sees her street. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 3, and study one sentence closely. Today’s question: what does a closed shop tell us about what is happening in Copenhagen?
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move is about objects. A lock or a sign is a small thing on the page, but someone with power put it there. So when you see one, ask two questions. Who did this? And who is it aimed at? The answer to the second one is where the danger is.
transcripts.dol: The model sentence names a person and a place, and every capital in it is there for a reason. The sentence to fix is really two sentences run together. Find where the first thought ends. One name also needs a mark to show that something belongs to someone.
transcripts.guide1: Today you build. In grammar and spelling, you’ll type the right word or letter yourself instead of choosing it. There’s a word bank to help. Watch out for the apostrophe trap in grammar, and in spelling, say a related word to hear the hidden letter.
transcripts.morphology: The Big Dipper is finished. Today we cross the sky to a smaller group of stars. The two roots are the same: one breaks, one leads. Two of today’s words begin with a part that means away or off, so read every meaning all the way to the end.
transcripts.vocabulary: Match the four words again. This time, before you tap a meaning, say it out loud in your own words. If you can explain a word to someone else, it belongs to you now.
transcripts.grammar: Each sentence is missing one owner-word. The word bank has four choices, and none of them needs an apostrophe. If you feel like adding one, stop. Ask yourself: does it mean it is, or they are? If not, leave the apostrophe out.
transcripts.spelling: Each word is missing the quiet letter in the middle. Don’t guess by sound, because the sound won’t tell you. Say the related word next to it, the one where that part is loud and clear. Then type the letter you hear.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about noticing. A locked shop is easy to walk past without a word. Annemarie doesn’t walk past. She asks her parents what it means. In my Copenhagen, many grown-ups looked away, because looking away felt safer. Paying attention, and asking the hard question, is its own kind of brave.
transcripts.read: Watch the shop door closely: what is on it, and what language is the sign written in? Then, at home, notice who comes to visit, and what time it is when he arrives. Notice how the grown-ups talk to each other in front of the girls. Stop at each pause question.
transcripts.rwm: Today’s sentence names a feeling but hides the reason. The writer uses one vague word, something, and that makes you lean in and guess. That’s how suspense works. When you write your own, tell your reader how it felt, but keep the why a secret.
transcripts.guide3: Time to write. The first question asks you to describe the shop door, so use details from the chapter. The second asks why the Germans closed certain shops. The third asks about Peter’s visit. Then you’ll give your claim three strong reasons.
transcripts.chapter: For the last question, think about Peter’s visit as a clue. It isn’t only who he is. It’s when he comes, and how the grown-ups behave once he’s there. A visit at that hour, in a city with rules about being out at night, tells you something.
transcripts.workshop: Your claim says what you think. Today you add three reasons that say why. Look at how Sam turns one big reason into three specific ones, each about something different Annemarie does. Make each of your reasons a clear sentence of its own.

a.raw: peter came to the apartment he brought news for annemaries papa
a.fixed: Peter came to the apartment. He brought news for Annemarie’s papa.
a.why: A capital P on Peter, a period after apartment, a capital H to start the second sentence, a capital A on Annemarie, an apostrophe-s on Annemarie’s, and a period at the end.

b.raw: mrs hirsch was gone the shop on annemaries corner was locked
b.fixed: Mrs. Hirsch was gone. The shop on Annemarie’s corner was locked.
b.why: A capital M and a period on Mrs., a capital H on Hirsch, a period after gone, a capital T to start the second sentence, an apostrophe-s on Annemarie’s, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain why the sign being in German makes it more frightening.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain what this new rule shows about where things are heading.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say what Annemarie might guess from the way the grown-ups act.

g4w16ff1.h1: The Johansens own the apartment, and there is more than one of them. Which owner-word goes before a noun?
g4w16ff1.why: their sits before the noun apartment and shows that it belongs to the Johansens.

g4w16ff2.h1: The necklace belongs to a girl, and no noun comes after the blank. Which word stands alone?
g4w16ff2.why: hers stands alone and needs no apostrophe.

g4w16ff3.h1: The lights belong to the city. Which word means belonging to it, with no apostrophe?
g4w16ff3.why: its shows belonging. It’s, with an apostrophe, would mean it is.

g4w16ff4.h1: The soldiers act as if the street belongs to them, and nothing comes after the blank.
g4w16ff4.why: theirs stands alone at the end of the sentence and needs no apostrophe.

s4w16ff1.h1: Say the related word separation. Which vowel is loud in the middle?
s4w16ff1.why: a: separate. You can hear it in separation.

s4w16ff2.h1: Say reside. Which vowel do you hear in the middle?

s4w16ff3.h1: Say govern. Which vowel comes right after the v?

s4w16ff4.h1: Say official. Which vowel do you hear after the f sounds?

match.interrupt: Interrupt has the root that means break. Look for the meaning about stopping something in the middle.
match.conduct: Conduct has the root that means lead. Look for the meaning about how someone behaves, or leads.
match.relocate: Relocate is about place: loc means place, re means again. Look for the meaning about moving somewhere new.
match.suspicion: Suspicion is a feeling, not an action. Look for the meaning about sensing that something is wrong.

wordgame.h: The bowl of the Little Dipper
wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Each right word clears the clouds and a star comes out.

why.t: This book is called Number the Stars. In Denmark, the Big Dipper has its own name: Karlsvognen, Charles’s Wagon. rupt means to break, so each right word breaks a cloud apart and a star shines through. duct and duce mean to lead, so each new star leads the line on to the next. One part of the sky each lesson, until it is full.

wordgame.winDay: The bowl of Lille Bjørn, the Little Bear, is shining. The next lesson’s words climb its handle.
wordgame.win: Every star is out. Follow the two stars at the front of Karlsvognen’s bowl: they lead your eye straight to the North Star, the star sailors have steered by for thousands of years. rupt = break, duct and duce = lead.

notes.wgrd: Objects can be warnings. When you see a lock, a sign or an empty chair, ask who put it there and who it is aimed at.
vocab: To stop something while it is happening.
How someone behaves or acts, or to lead or guide.
To move someone or something to a new place, sometimes by force.
A feeling that something is wrong, even if you don’t have proof.
notes.wordParts: rupt means “to break” (interrupt, erupt). duct and duce mean “to lead” or “to bring” (conduct, introduce).
notes.grammar: Possessive pronouns show who owns something. Some sit before a noun (her coat, their house); some stand alone (the coat is hers). They never take an apostrophe: it’s means “it is” and they’re means “they are.”
notes.spelling: In a long word, a vowel you say quickly can fade into a soft /uh/ sound called a schwa, so you can’t hear which letter spells it. Find a related word where that part is loud: separate → separation, government → govern.

case.title: A Kitchen in the War Years
case.alt: A small, dim kitchen rebuilt in a museum, with an old radio on a shelf, a sink with a checked curtain, and a two-ring gas burner on a little table.
label: The Museum of Danish Resistance rebuilt this kitchen to show how an ordinary Copenhagen family lived during the occupation.

Look for the little two-ring burner on the table and the radio on the shelf. In Chapter 3, electricity is rationed, so the Johansens light candles at night, and Mama sometimes cooks on a small stove. Coal and gas were short too, so a warm kitchen was precious.

look.q: What would this family use the radio for?
look.a: Listening to the news. Many Danes secretly tuned in to the BBC from London, which the Germans did not want them to hear.

look.q: Why is the room so dim?
look.a: Light cost electricity, and electricity was rationed. At night, windows also had to be covered so no light showed outside.

case.credit: A reconstructed wartime kitchen at Frihedsmuseet (Museum of Danish Resistance), Copenhagen. Photo: Leif Jørgensen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
